Opossum cranial measurements and a genomic relationship matrix

Source: R/data.R
opossum.Rd

Cranial Euclidean distances and individual information for opossums from the colony of the South Texas Diabetes and Obesity Institute, analysed by Porto et al. (2016). The traits are the same 35 landmarks as ratones_morpho, so the two datasets can be compared directly.

Usage

opossum

Format

Two objects.

opossum

a data frame with 553 rows and 38 columns: id, sex, age in days, and the 35 cranial distances as measured, named after the landmarks they span, with underscores as in ratones_morpho. Row names are the individual IDs. 22 individuals are missing every trait. lmm_animal accepts fully missing response rows, but they must be removed before fitting lm_phen_cov. 505 individuals have no missing value in any trait or covariate.

opossum_grm

a 553 by 553 genomic relationship matrix computed from 3,696 markers as \(ZZ^\top / (2\sum_j p_j(1-p_j))\) (VanRaden 2008), \(Z\) being the allele-count matrix centred by twice the sample allele frequencies \(p_j\). It equals genomic_relationship() applied to the markers, and it is on the scale of a pedigree relationship matrix, so G fitted on it is the additive genetic covariance of the population. Rows and columns are named with the individual IDs of opossum, so the rows of the subset being analysed can be passed as the A argument of lmm_animal directly, as in the example. The full matrix is only positive semidefinite, so pass blend_A = TRUE if it is given whole. The diagonal runs from 0.64 to 1.70 with a mean of 1.05, and the off-diagonal entries average zero, since the allele frequencies come from the same animals. Versions up to 0.8.1 shipped the same matrix divided by the number of markers instead, 2.86 times smaller, which inflated G and the heritabilities fitted on it.

Source

Porto, A., Schmelter, R., VandeBerg, J. L., Marroig, G., & Cheverud, J. M. (2016). Evolution of the genotype-to-phenotype map and the cost of pleiotropy in mammals. Genetics, 204(4), 1601-1612. doi:10.1534/genetics.116.189431 . Data deposited on figshare as “Data - Genetics - Porto et al 2016”, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.4055961 .

The coded marker files in that archive carry no individual identifiers, so the animals are matched to the cranial measurements by row order. The two sources agree in length at 553, and the identities are attached here as the row and column names of opossum_grm.

Details

Unlike the mice, these animals carry marker genotypes, so the relationship matrix is genomic rather than genealogical. That matters for these data: the colony pedigree shipped with the original archive gives every pair a kinship coefficient between 0.69 and 0.93, which leaves additive variance indistinguishable from a shared colony effect. The genomic matrix separates relatives from non-relatives and makes the genetic covariance identifiable.

The distances are stored as measured. Porto et al. (2016) analysed them untransformed, and the phenomenon is confirmed by their published phenotypic covariance, whose diagonal correlates 0.834 with the variances of the raw distances against 0.046 with those of their logarithms.

References

Porto, A., Schmelter, R., VandeBerg, J. L., Marroig, G., & Cheverud, J. M. (2016). Evolution of the genotype-to-phenotype map and the cost of pleiotropy in mammals. Genetics, 204(4), 1601-1612. doi:10.1534/genetics.116.189431

See also

ratones_morpho, lmm_animal

Examples

data(opossum)
dim(opossum)
#> [1] 553  38
dim(opossum_grm)
#> [1] 553 553
traits <- setdiff(names(opossum), c("id", "sex", "age"))
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Phenotypic covariance of four traits, no pedigree needed
lm_phen_cov(as.matrix(opossum[, traits[1:4]]),
            model.matrix(~ sex + age, opossum))

# Genomic animal model on the same four traits
design <- animal_design(
  stats::reformulate(c("sex", "age"),
                     response = sprintf("cbind(%s)", paste(traits[1:4],
                                                           collapse = ", "))),
  data = opossum, pedigree = NULL)
lmm_animal(design$Y, design$X, opossum_grm[rownames(design$Y),
                                           rownames(design$Y)])
} # }
